passage: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a material medium to propagate, meaning it cannot travel through the vacuum of space regardless of how intense the vibration is. When sound travels, it creates regions of high pressure called compressions and regions of low pressure called rarefactions, where air particles are simply spread further apart rather than being completely absent. The speed at which sound moves depends entirely on the properties of the medium, such as density and elasticity, rather than the frequency of the wave. Because particles in solids are packed more tightly than in gases, sound travels significantly faster through solid materials than through air. Furthermore, sound waves are longitudinal, meaning the particles of the medium oscillate back and forth parallel to the direction of wave propagation, not up and down like waves on a string. It is important to distinguish between physical characteristics: loudness is determined by the amplitude of the vibration, while pitch is determined by the frequency. Finally, ultrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies above the human audible range, which remains inaudible to us no matter how much the volume is increased.

items.evidence: The speed at which sound moves depends entirely on the properties of the medium, such as density and elasticity, rather than the frequency of the wave.
items.q: A singer sings the same note in a hall, first at higher frequency. What happens to the sound's speed?
options: It stays the same in the same air
It rises as the frequency rises
It falls as the frequency rises
It becomes constant like light's speed
items.explain: Speed depends on the medium, not the frequency, so the same air gives the same speed.

wrong.why: thinks higher frequency means faster speed
reverses the relation between frequency and speed
thinks speed of sound is a universal constant

items.evidence: When sound travels, it creates regions of high pressure called compressions and regions of low pressure called rarefactions, where air particles are simply spread further apart rather than being completely absent.
items.q: What is true about the air in a rarefaction as a sound passes?
options: Its particles are farther apart than usual
Its particles are fully removed from the place
Its particles are packed tighter than usual
Its particles stop moving for a moment
items.explain: A rarefaction is low pressure where particles are spread further apart, not a region without any particles.

wrong.why: thinks a rarefaction has no particles at all
thinks low pressure means particles stop

items.evidence: Because particles in solids are packed more tightly than in gases, sound travels significantly faster through solid materials than through air.
items.q: Why does sound travel faster through a steel rail than through the air?
options: Its particles are packed more tightly together
Its particles are too dense to let sound pass
Its particles are spread farther apart than air
Its particles move up and down as the sound passes
items.explain: Particles packed tightly in solids pass the vibration along faster, so sound moves faster than in air.

wrong.why: thinks density blocks sound in solids
reverses the particle spacing in solids and gases
thinks sound moves particles up and down

items.evidence: Finally, ultrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies above the human audible range, which remains inaudible to us no matter how much the volume is increased.
items.q: An ultrasound machine is made much louder. What will a person standing nearby hear?
options: Nothing, as its frequency is too high
A loud sound that hurts the ears
A faint sound, only if close enough
A loud sound, but only at low pitch
items.explain: Ultrasound is above the human audible range, so it stays inaudible however loud it is made.

wrong.why: thinks ultrasound is just very loud sound
thinks high volume makes ultrasound audible
